rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.9 describe a two-season (2016-17, 2017-18) randomized block field experiment with four replicates in a farmer's field at Gosaba, West Bengal, comparing surface irrigation with drip irrigation at 100% and 80% ET0 with/without straw mulch on tomato. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 4 report fruit yield of 56.51 (drip 100% ET0) and 53.00 t/ha (drip 80% ET0) versus 43.37 t/ha under surface irrigation, and marketable yield 55.19 and 49.94 vs 39.38 t/ha; the Discussion states drip irrigation with less water gave higher marketable yield than surface irrigation.
rows.notes: The study's own result is on drip vs surface irrigation in a water-scarce coastal saline dry-season setting, not under drought per se; the passage's 'drought conditions' framing is the review's. Yield measured by one method (plot harvest) at one site with one cultivar. Post-harvest soil EC (Table 9), leaf N/K and chlorophyll (Table 5) were measured, but the asserted yield mechanism (optimal root-zone soil moisture, reduced nutrient losses, better root development) is not measured and is supported by citations, so Q4 is conservatively no. No explicit conditions or limitations of the result are stated; only means with DMRT letters and significance stars, no SD/SE/CI.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.9 describe a two-season replicated field experiment at Gosaba, West Bengal comparing surface and drip irrigation treatments on tomato. Q2: Section 3.8 and Table 12 report irrigation applied of 236.07/222.74 mm (drip 80% ET0) and 295.08/278.43 mm (drip 100% ET0) versus 300 mm for surface irrigation in years 1/2, lower total water use under drip, and water productivity of 151-186 kg/ha-mm under drip versus 105-116 under surface irrigation.
rows.notes: Water saving under drip is largely determined by the scheduling design (ET0-based volumes vs fixed 5 cm applications at critical stages), but the study does report its own water-use accounting and resulting water productivity. Single site, single crop, single accounting method; no measurement of evaporation or percolation as intermediate variables; no stated conditions, limitations or dispersion measures for the water-use result.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.9 describe a two-season replicated field experiment at Gosaba, West Bengal with five treatments including drip at 80% ET0 + straw mulch. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 4 report that drip irrigation at 80% ET0 + straw mulch gave the significantly highest fruit yield (61.67 t/ha) and marketable yield (60.32 t/ha), versus 43.37 and 39.38 t/ha under surface irrigation; Section 3.8 reports 58.58 and 61.44 t/ha in years 1 and 2 for this treatment; Conclusions state the combination enhanced fruit number and marketable yield.
rows.notes: Passage matches the study's own result directly (drip + straw mulch enhanced tomato yield). Yield from one method at one site with one cultivar over two seasons. Soil EC, leaf nutrients, chlorophyll and microbial counts were measured, but the yield mechanism is asserted/cited rather than tested through soil moisture, so Q4 is conservatively no. The authors note the salinity/microbial benefit was restricted to the top-soil layer, but no limitation of the yield result itself is stated. Only treatment means with DMRT letters; no SD/SE/CI.

notes: Full text available; some pages have OCR overlap in the Introduction/Methods but all results tables are readable. Study is a single-site, two-season field experiment on tomato in the coastal saline Ganges Delta.
